lessonTitle: Title Blocks, Line Types and Standards

blocks.text: A US contractor receives a drawing from a European supplier, reads its top view as a bottom view and measures a bracket in inches when the dimensions were in millimetres. Two conventions, both properly followed, produced a scrapped part.

blocks.markdown: A drawing is a legal instruction to make a part. To be unambiguous it must follow a **standard**: ISO (the International Organization for Standardization, widely used in Europe and Asia) or ASME (the American Society of Mechanical Engineers, the US convention). The two standards agree on far more than they differ. This unit covers three things: the **title block**, the **line types**, and where **ISO and ASME conventions differ**.

blocks.title: Title block
blocks.text: The **title block** is a table, normally in the bottom right corner of the sheet, that identifies the drawing and its status. It lets someone who has only the sheet find out what the part is, who owns it, which version it is, and how to read it.

rows: Unique identifier; links to the BOM
Ratio of drawing size to real size
First or third angle, so views are read correctly
Default unit (usually mm) and tolerance for undimensioned sizes
What the part is made from and its surface treatment
Position in a set and version of the drawing
blocks.caption: Typical required title block fields

blocks.title: Choosing a scale
blocks.prompt: A part is 600 mm long and 250 mm wide. It must fit in a drawing area 380 mm by 260 mm on an A3 sheet. Which preferred scale (1:1, 1:2, 1:5) should be used and what are the sizes on paper?

steps.text: At 1:1 the length is 600 mm, which is larger than 380 mm: too big.
Both fit within 380 mm by 260 mm. 1:5 would also fit but would waste space and make detail smaller.

blocks.answer: Use 1:2: the part appears 300 mm by 125 mm on paper. The scale goes in the title block; dimensions still show real sizes.

blocks.markdown: **Line types.** Drawings are legible because each line type has a job. Thick lines carry the outline; thin lines carry everything supporting. A typical ratio of thick to thin line width is about 2 to 1.

rows: Edges and outlines you can see
Axes of holes, shafts and symmetry
Thin chain, thick at ends and bends, with arrows
Marks where a section is cut and the viewing direction
blocks.caption: Line types

blocks.markdown: **ISO and ASME compared.** Both systems use millimetre or inch units, both use the same basic line types, and both place the same title-block information on the sheet. They differ in several habits:

rows: Decimal marker on inch/metric values below 1
Inch drawings: no leading zero (.500); metric drawings: leading zero (0.5)
Inch drawings carry trailing zeros to match the tolerance
blocks.caption: Representative differences between ISO and ASME conventions

blocks.title: Converting an ASME dimension
blocks.prompt: An ASME drawing gives a hole spacing of 2.750 in. State the equivalent on a metric ISO drawing and note two other conventions to change.

steps.text: Third-angle views must be checked: if the drawing is reissued in first angle, the arrangement of views and the projection symbol change.
Decimal values below one are written with a leading zero (0.5, not .5) on a metric drawing.

blocks.answer: 69.85 mm; also check the projection symbol and use a leading zero.

blocks.title: Never assume the projection
blocks.text: If the symbol is missing the drawing is ambiguous. A reader must never guess, because a wrong guess swaps the top and bottom views and the left and right side views.

items: Fill every title block field, especially number, scale, units, material and issue.
Use thick lines for outlines and thin lines for the rest.
State the projection and the units on the sheet.
Do not mix ISO and ASME habits on one drawing.

points: The title block identifies the drawing: number, title, scale, projection, units, tolerance, material, responsibility and issue.
Use thick continuous for visible edges, thin dashed for hidden, thin chain for centres, and chain with thick ends for cutting planes.
ISO and ASME differ mainly in projection angle, default units and decimal conventions.

questions.stem: Which title-block field uniquely identifies a drawing and links it to the bill of materials?
questions.explanation: The number is the unique key used in the BOM and in orders. The other fields describe the drawing but do not identify it uniquely.

questions.stem: Which line type is used for hidden edges?
questions.explanation: Hidden edges are thin and dashed. Chain lines are for centres and cutting planes.

questions.stem: A drawing at scale 1:4 shows a flange with a measured length of 36 mm on paper. Calculate the real length of the flange in mm.
questions.explanation: At scale 1:4 the real size is 4 times the paper size: 36 x 4 = 144 mm. Dimensions on the drawing would still show the real sizes.

questions.stem: An ASME drawing gives a dimension of 3.500 in. Convert to millimetres, using 1 in = 25.4 mm.
questions.explanation: 3.500 x 25.4 = 88.9 mm. The same part on an ISO drawing would be dimensioned as 88.9 mm (or rounded as the tolerance allows).

questions.stem: How is a cutting plane line for a section drawn?

options.text: Thin chain with thick ends and arrows

questions.correctOptionText: Thin chain with thick ends and arrows
questions.explanation: The cutting plane line is a chain line, thick at the ends and direction changes, with arrows to show the viewing direction and letters to label it. Visible outlines are thick continuous, not chain.

questions.stem: Which projection is typical of ASME drawings?
questions.explanation: ASME (US) drawings normally use third-angle projection; ISO traditionally uses first angle. Always read the symbol.

questions.stem: An inch-based ASME drawing needs a dimension of one half inch with a tolerance of +/-0.005 in. Which presentation follows ASME inch convention?

distractorRationale.c: Fraction not used with the tolerance.

questions.explanation: ASME inch drawings omit the leading zero for values less than one and use trailing zeros to match the tolerance, so .500 +/-.005. An ISO or metric drawing would use a leading zero.

questions.stem: List five fields that must appear in a title block and state the purpose of each.
markingGuide: Scale: relates drawing size to real size
Projection symbol: how to read the views
questions.explanation: Five valid fields with a stated purpose each earn the credit. Each point in the marking guide earns credit, so state every point explicitly and give its reason.

questions.stem: Compare ISO and ASME conventions for projection symbol and dimension units, explaining the risk if a reader assumes the wrong convention.
markingGuide: ISO traditionally first angle; ASME third angle
ISO millimetres by default; ASME often inches
Wrong projection swaps top/bottom and left/right views
Wrong units give a size error of 25.4 times
Both state the convention on the sheet; read the symbol and units note
questions.explanation: A full answer gives both differences and the consequence of misreading. Each point in the marking guide earns credit, so state every point explicitly and give its reason.

questions.stem: A centre line is drawn as a thin chain line with alternating long and short dashes.
questions.explanation: Centre lines are thin chain lines, with long dashes alternating with short ones, marking axes of symmetry. They are not part of the visible outline.
